name: Ipalapa Amuzgo
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [pp.12-13] El acento tónico permanece invariablemente en la raiz principal de la palabra. Cuando ésta está formada de varias raices, cada una de ellas lleva el acento tónico, de lo que resulta que una palabra tiene uno, dos y mas acentos. Como: kètsuè, perro, el acento tónico en la e final. tchintsi tiòhò: enredar, el tónico en las palabras tsi y hó. tchininkià nawi, envenenar, el acento tonico en las sílabas kiá y wi. [p.4] El sistema de prefijos domina en el amuzgo, siendo generalmente la raís principal la última sílaba de la palabra.
new_statements.translation: [pp.12-13] The tonic accent remains invariably on the principal root of the word. When the word is formed from several roots, each of them carries the tonic accent, so that a word has one, two or more accents. E.g. kètsuè 'dog', the tonic accent on the final e; tchintsi tiòhò 'to entangle', the tonic on tsi and hó; tchininkià nawi 'to poison', the tonic accent on the syllables kiá and wi. [p.4] The prefix system dominates in Amuzgo, the principal root generally being the last syllable of the word.
new_statements.citation: Belmar, Francisco. 1901. Investigación sobre el idioma amuzgo, que se habla en algunos pueblos del Distrito de Jamiltepec. Se toma para dichas investigaciones el idioma que se habla en el Pueblo de Ipalapa. (Lenguas del Estado de Oaxaca.) Oaxaca. 163 pp.
new_statements.locator: section 'Acento', pp. 12-13 (page images); supporting sentence p. 4 ('Clasificación morfológica'), image
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the (principal) root; since Amuzgo morphology is prefixing and the root is generally the word-final syllable, stress normally surfaces on the last syllable (kètsuè 'dog', stress on final e). In words/compounds built from more than one root, each root syllable carries a stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such; multi-root words are said to carry one tonic accent per root ('uno, dos y mas acentos').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the multi-root case; p.6 adds that short vowels are hurried over 'to rest on the last natural or long vowel of the word'. p.5 separately notes a lexically distinctive pitch 'acento'/'canto' (tone) that the orthography does not represent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement from isolated citation forms in a 1901 pre-phonemic description; Belmar marks stressed 'natural' vowels with an acute (p.7) but also uses grave/circumflex for short/nasal vowels, so his diacritics are not purely stress marks. The language is tonal (Belmar p.5; all modern Amuzgo descriptions), so 'tonal-with-stress-statement' would be an equally defensible tag; the positional content is root = generally final syllable, consistent with Buck 2018 for Xochistlahuaca Amuzgo (stress on last syllable of the stem).
new_statements.identity_note: Belmar's title page states the data are 'el idioma que se habla en el Pueblo de Ipalapa' (Santa María Ipalapa, Distrito de Jamiltepec, Oaxaca), i.e. exactly Ipalapa Amuzgo [azm], ipal1235 — not San Pedro Amuzgos Amuzgo (sanp1260) or Guerrero Amuzgo (guer1243), which he names only as neighbouring Amuzgo towns. Modern Amuzgo phonologies on file (Buck 2018, Do Bui 2018, de Jesús García 2019, Apóstol Polanco 2024) all describe Guerrero varieties and explicitly say the Ipalapa variety has no modern phonological study.

sources.note: 'Fonetismo' pp.5-13 with a section 'Acento' pp.12-13: the tonic accent stays invariably on the principal root of the word; words built from several roots carry an accent on each root (kètsuè 'perro', accent on final e). p.4: the language is prefixing and the principal root is generally the last syllable of the word. p.5: a further 'acento'/'canto' (i.e. tone) distinguishes words written alike and cannot be represented in writing. p.6: short vowels are passed over quickly 'para descansar en la última natural ó larga de la palabra'.

sources.note: About Xochistlahuaca; pp.124-125 state that for the Santa María Ipalapa variety 'no hay ningún registro de este tipo de análisis' (no phonological analysis exists).

sources.citation: Buck, Marjorie J. 2018. Gramática del amuzgo de Xochistlahuaca, Guerrero. Serie de gramáticas de lenguas indígenas de México 16. México: ILV. (Guerrero Amuzgo, guer1243)
sources.note: Describes a different variety (Xochistlahuaca): §2.4.2 every word has one syllable bearing the prosodic accent, generally the last syllable of the stem. For Ipalapa it only says the variety was not in the 1971 SIL intelligibility survey and 'según Belmar (1901), difiere en algunos aspectos'; bibliography B.4 lists Belmar 1901 and Cuevas Suárez 2010 as the only works on Ipalapa Amuzgo.
